title: NCLT Hyderabad Orders Substantive Consolidation Of Two Group Companies' CIRPs
seo_title: NCLT Merges Two Linked Companies' Insolvency Cases
meta_description: NCLT Hyderabad orders substantive consolidation of Panduranga Energy Systems' and GMP Infrastructure's separate CIRPs, citing shared land and creditors.
court: National Company Law Tribunal, Hyderabad Bench
case_name: Union Bank of India v. Panduranga Energy Systems Private Limited (consolidated with GMP Infrastructure Private Limited's CIRP)
citation: IA (IBC) No. 1398 of 2026 in CP (IB) No. 304/7/HDB/2022
body: Running two separate insolvency processes for companies joined at the hip rarely makes commercial sense, and the NCLT's Hyderabad Bench has now said so plainly in ordering the two corporate insolvency resolution processes of Panduranga Energy Systems Private Limited and GMP Infrastructure Private Limited to be run as one. The application for substantive consolidation came from Union Bank of India, a financial creditor common to both companies, in proceedings already pending as CP (IB) No. 304/7/HDB/2022.

The Tribunal, through Member (Judicial) Rajeev Bhardwaj, grounded its decision in the physical and financial entanglement between the two entities rather than in any abstract preference for administrative convenience. GMP Infrastructure owns the land on which the relevant plant and shared infrastructure sit, and that same land secured facilities extended to Panduranga Energy Systems, alongside a corporate guarantee GMP had given for Panduranga's borrowings. Running the two insolvency processes in parallel but separately risked a resolution applicant for one company ending up unable to access land or infrastructure controlled by the other, which would have depressed the realisable value achievable in either process.

A second factor weighed heavily with the Bench: the financial creditors in both companies' insolvency proceedings turned out to be identical. Where the same set of lenders is owed money by both entities and the same underlying assets secure both sets of debt, keeping the processes apart invites exactly the kind of coordination problems, duplicated claims and competing resolution plans that substantive consolidation exists to prevent.

The order does not simply merge paperwork. It directs that pending claims and proceedings in both companies' separate processes be folded into the single consolidated CIRP going forward, and it leaves room for a fresh Form G, the public invitation for resolution plans, to be issued if the resolution professional considers it necessary now that the asset pool and claim set look different from how either process looked on its own. Kalvakota Venkat Narsinga Rao, who had been administering one or both of the separate processes, continues as the resolution professional for the consolidated proceeding.

Substantive consolidation is not something the IBC spells out as a routine remedy, and tribunals have generally reserved it for cases where the corporate veil between group companies has worn thin enough that treating them as separate economic units no longer reflects commercial reality. Shared land, a corporate guarantee running from one entity to the other's lender, and an identical creditor base across both companies are the kind of facts tribunals have pointed to in other cases to justify the step, and this order follows that pattern rather than departing from it. Separate resolution professionals running two overlapping processes over the same physical plant would in any event have had to coordinate constantly on access to the land and the shared infrastructure sitting on it, duplicating effort that a single consolidated process avoids altogether.

Creditors in each of the two separate proceedings will now find their claims folded into one combined process rather than voted on twice in two different committees of creditors, which also removes the risk of the two committees arriving at inconsistent views on how the shared assets ought to be valued or distributed. That risk is not hypothetical in group insolvencies of this kind, where a lender sitting on both committees could otherwise find itself negotiating against its own interests in one process while trying to maximise recovery in the other.

For lenders financing group structures where one company's assets effectively backstop another's borrowing, this order is a reminder that the structure itself can become the basis for consolidating what might otherwise have been kept as two distinct recovery processes. A bank holding exposure to both entities in a tightly linked group has an argument, grounded in exactly these facts, for seeking consolidation rather than fighting two insolvency processes on two separate tracks with competing claims on the same underlying asset.

Resolution applicants interested in either company will now have to bid for the consolidated whole rather than picking off one entity while leaving the other, and its claims against the shared land and guarantee, as someone else's problem. Whether that produces a higher realisation than two separate sales would have is precisely the commercial judgment the Tribunal's order is betting on, and it is the resolution professional's task now to test that judgment through a single, combined process rather than two overlapping ones.
why_it_matters: Group companies often share land, guarantees and lenders in ways that make running separate insolvency processes for each entity impractical and value-destroying. This order shows the test tribunals apply before ordering substantive consolidation, shared assets, a corporate guarantee linking the two debts, and an identical creditor base, and gives lenders exposed to tightly linked group structures a template for seeking the same relief elsewhere.
card_summary: NCLT Hyderabad orders substantive consolidation of Panduranga Energy Systems' and GMP Infrastructure's separate CIRPs, citing shared land, a corporate guarantee and an identical creditor base.
card_tip: A lender exposed to two group companies sharing land, a guarantee and the same creditors can seek substantive consolidation of their separate CIRPs rather than running two competing processes.
verification_notes: The case name, citation (IA (IBC) No. 1398 of 2026 in CP (IB) No. 304/7/HDB/2022), the bench (Rajeev Bhardwaj, Member Judicial), the applicant (Union Bank of India), the facts relied on (GMP Infrastructure's ownership of the land, the corporate guarantee it gave for Panduranga's facilities, and the identical creditor base across both companies), the direction to fold pending claims into the consolidated process with a fresh Form G if needed, and the resolution professional's name (Kalvakota Venkat Narsinga Rao) are confirmed from LiveLawBiz's report, read against the underlying order document LiveLawBiz separately published. A second, independent news report of this specific order could not be located in this run; the order document itself is treated as the near-primary source relied on in its place, consistent with the approach taken where only one reporter has covered a specific order. No information on the companies' debt amounts, the number of creditors involved, or any appeal against the order was available in the sources reviewed and is therefore left out.
